transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Rivera, thank you for coming back to the room to talk with me. I have some news about your medication that is quite serious, and I want to be very direct with you. We made a mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Three days ago, I wrote in your chart that you should stop taking the blood thinner, but I didn't notify the pharmacy. Because of that, you kept receiving and taking a medication that you should have stopped. I am very sorry. I take full responsibility for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I did feel a bit dizzy. But maybe that is just the illness. I have been sick for a while.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand why you might think that, but the dizziness is likely happening because you have too much of that medication in your system. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess. I just do not want to cause any trouble. I am not here to complain.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are not causing any trouble, Mr. Rivera. It is my job to make sure your medicine is correct, and I failed to do that. I am truly sorry for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is okay. I know the hospital is busy. Maybe my body is just reacting to the infection.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is possible the infection is playing a part, but the fact remains that you took a drug for three extra days that you shouldn't have. I don't want to brush that off as part of your illness because it was a mistake on my part.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just don't want this to be a big deal. I don't have... I don't have a certain kind of paperwork. I don't want my records to show I am a problem.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be very clear about this. This mistake has nothing to do with your status or your paperwork. It was my error, and it will be documented as my error. You are not a problem, and your care here is our priority regardless of anything else.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You really think it was the medicine?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. Based on the dosage you received, that is the most likely cause. Is there any part of that which feels confusing?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. I just thought it was just the way things go when you are sick.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: This is a heavy thing to process. I can see you are being very patient with me, and I know it's uncomfortable to hear that we messed up your treatment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to get better.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the most important thing. We have a plan to fix this now. First, I have already called the pharmacy and the medication has been removed from your room. Second, I am ordering a blood test right now to see exactly how much of the drug is still in your system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When will that happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The nurse will be in here within the hour to draw your blood. Then, I will come back this afternoon, around 3:00, to give you the results and tell you how we will manage the recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what about the future?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am going to meet with my supervisor to change how we notify the pharmacy so this doesn't happen to another patient. While we wait for the test, I need you to tell me immediately if you notice any new bruising or if the dizziness gets worse. Can you do that for me?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Thank you. I will be back at 3:00. If you think of any other questions before then, please hit the call button.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish all turns, maintains a regulated pace during the patient's anxiety about paperwork, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: Error named in the first turn, lay language used throughout, and comprehension checked twice ('Does that make sense so far?' and 'Is there any part of that which feels confusing?').

A.justification: Direct apologies used multiple times, resident takes full personal responsibility, and maintains accountability even when the patient tries to excuse the error.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('uncomfortable', 'heavy thing to process') and engages the patient's specific concerns regarding their status and paperwork.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (blood test, pharmacy call), timelines (within the hour, 3:00), patient role (report bruising/dizziness), and prevention (meeting with supervisor).
